column4: Bea is sure every one of these people thinks she's a disaster.
And this week, she can hear exactly what they're thinking. Let's rewind to Monday.
This is Bea. She makes the best cinnamon buns on Crumb Island. She also still replays something awkward she said four years ago. Most nights.
And on Monday morning, Bea woke up able to hear every honest thought anyone had about her.
Three rules. One: if someone thinks about you, you hear it. Two: it lasts seven days. Three: the catch. In very, very small print.
Day one. Bea braced herself for a flood.
Ooh. Cinnamon.
Those buns look incredible.
That was it. All day. Two thoughts. Both about the buns.
Psychologists call this the spotlight effect. In one study, students wore an embarrassing T-shirt into a room. They guessed about half the people there would remember it. Only about a quarter did.
Enjoy your day!
You too! ...Wait.
Day two. Bea replayed that "you too" about forty times.
He thinks you're so weird.
And what did he actually think?
Nothing. He'd forgotten before he reached the door.
This one's called the illusion of transparency. We assume our nerves show on the outside. Usually, people see much less than we think.
Which brings us back to day three.
Oof. That happens to me all the time.
Is she okay?
I should help.
Research suggests we expect people to judge our slip-ups more harshly than they really do. Partly because everyone watching has dropped a tray of their own.
Theo brought a broom. Mo brought a sandwich. Nobody knows why.
Day four. Bea's mum came to visit.
Bea had always believed her mum was a little disappointed. A bakery. Not the life she'd hoped for.
So Bea listened.
I'm so proud of her. I've just never known how to say it.
Day five. Not every thought was kind.
The buns are a bit dry today.
Ouch. And that's real. Some people will think critical things. But notice what it was about. The buns. Not Bea's worth as a person.
Day six. Bea did something brave. She told her mum she missed her.
Showing vulnerability can feel like weakness. But researchers found we judge our own vulnerable moments far more harshly than the same moments in other people.
Day seven. The quietest day yet. Except for one voice that hadn't stopped all week.
Remember rule three? The very small print?
Every thought about you. Including your own.
They're laughing at you.
You always mess things up.
Why are you like this?
All week, the harshest voice on Crumb Island wasn't a customer. It was Bea.

If that voice sounds familiar, you're not alone. Next time it starts, try answering it the way you'd answer a friend who just dropped a tray. In experiments, people who were kind to themselves after a mistake were more motivated to improve, not less.
Day eight. The thoughts were gone.
Oops. ...That's okay.
Most people are busy with their own lives. And when they do notice you, they're often kinder than the voice in your head.
